title: Philosophical terms
intro: A working vocabulary for this sequence — the words the sittings actually force — not a dictionary of all philosophy. Read the pages first; these are margins. Later thinkers reuse or invert an earlier word; the links are the point.

terms.short: Nature as what the world is made of, and how it moves — not the countryside.
terms.definition: The first philosophers used physis for the world’s inner constitution: the stuff or process that makes change intelligible. Milesians fight over water, the apeiron, and air because they are fighting over that. Aristotle later tightens it: nature is a principle of motion and rest in the thing itself, unlike an artifact whose principle is in the artisan.

terms.short: Nothing comes from nothing — so ‘birth’ and ‘death’ have to be explained some other way.
terms.definition: Generation cannot be a leap out of sheer non-being, nor destruction a drop into it. Milesians still tell process-stories under that ban; Parmenides uses it to threaten coming-to-be altogether; the pluralists and atomists save the appearances by making birth a rearrangement. Lucretius later turns the same rule into a therapy of fear.

terms.short: Anaximander’s indefinite: an origin that is not one of the opposites it would have to explain.
terms.definition: If the source were water or fire, it could not fairly account for its rivals. The apeiron — the unbounded, the indefinite — is a principle that is not a named element. That is why it is more ambitious than Thales’ water. It is not ‘infinity’ as a number.

terms.short: The common account of how things are, which people miss by living as if they had a private one.
terms.definition: In Heraclitus, logos is speech, measure, and the world’s order sounding together — not homework in ‘logic,’ and not an opinion you are entitled to. The many sleepwalk past what is common. Drop the word and keep only ‘flux,’ and the view collapses.

terms.short: Conflict as how things hold together, even as justice — not a glitch in an otherwise peaceful cosmos.
terms.definition: Heraclitus’s war is constitutive: opposition is the pattern, not an accident. Empedocles later splits Love and Strife into the moving causes of mixture and separation. ‘Everything changes’ is the wrong paraphrase if it erases structured conflict. Neither writer is celebrating violence for its own sake.

terms.short: What is, as opposed to what is not — and the refusal to make not-being a way of inquiry.
terms.definition: Parmenides: you cannot think or say what is not, so coming-to-be would be a passage through nothing, and what is is ungenerated and not many as mortals say. Aristotle studies being as being, said in many ways around substance. Heidegger insists that being is not a being among beings. One word, three pressures.

terms.short: How things show up — opinion, sense, seeming — as against what is, or against the object science names.
terms.definition: Parmenides contrasts the way of truth with mortal names and a deceptive cosmos. Pluralists and atomists then try to save appearances without violating ‘nothing from nothing.’ Russell’s table reopens it: what you immediately see is not simply the public table. Watch which contrast a sitting is using.

terms.short: Empty interval, without which uncuttable bodies cannot move.
terms.definition: Atomists need void because packed being cannot yield. It is ‘what is not’ put to work — the Eleatic scandal turned into a physics. Emptiness is a condition of motion, not a rival stuff. Without it there is no Epicurean consolation either.

terms.short: Ungenerated, uncuttable beings, differing by shape and arrangement, moving in void.
terms.definition: Atoms are little Parmenidean beings in the plural, with empty space for room. Qualities, life, and value are supposed to fall out of shape, order, and position — which is exactly what you still would not understand about an animal from a complete inventory. Lucretius makes the picture a consolation: if thunder is atoms, it is not a judgment.

terms.short: Mind: Anaxagoras’s arranger of mixture, and later Aristotle’s grasp of first principles.
terms.definition: Anaxagoras introduces Nous because order may require intelligence, not only stuff — the complaint is that the fragments never pay the promise. In the Posterior Analytics, nous is how undemonstrated first principles are known, because demonstration cannot go back forever. Do not hear a Cartesian inner theatre in either use.

terms.short: The one character by which pious things are pious — a definition, not a list of cases.
terms.definition: Socrates wants the form of piety: what it is, such that examples are examples of it. ‘What the gods love’ can be true of all pious things and still fail, because it does not give the why. Plato later hypostasizes Forms; Aristotle keeps form-in-matter as a cause and refuses a separate heaven of them.

terms.short: Do the gods love the pious because it is pious, or is it pious because they love it?
terms.definition: If piety is only what the gods love, their love looks arbitrary. If they love it because it is pious, piety is independent of their love. Euthyphro cannot hold both. The same fork returns whenever someone tries to rest the good on a command.

terms.short: Impasse: the definitions fail, and that failure is the result, not an accident.
terms.definition: Socratic dialogues often end without a formula. You have learned how the question must look, and that Euthyphro or Thrasymachus does not yet know. Republic I clears a site for later books; it does not already give justice in the soul. Aporia is not Plato getting tired, and not a proof that nothing can be said.

aliases: I know that I do not know
terms.short: Knowing that one lacks the wisdom others pretend to — a method and a stance, not nihilism.
terms.definition: The oracle frames the examinations of politicians, poets, and craftsmen. Socrates still claims things about death and duty; he will not quit philosophizing to buy acquittal. Mix this with total skepticism and you misread both the Apology and later Pyrrhonism.

terms.short: Disciplined question and answer — later, in Hegel, the movement of self-consciousness itself.
terms.definition: In Plato it is the highest stretch of the divided line: intelligence of Forms, not eristic scoring, beginning as public elenchus. Hegel uses the word for a necessary development: recognition cannot stay one-sided, and work transforms the bondsman. Mark the shift when you leave the Republic for the Phenomenology.

terms.short: Learning as recovering what the soul already knew — Plato’s bid to solve the paradox of inquiry.
terms.definition: Meno’s paradox: you cannot search for what you do not know, because you would not recognize it. Recollection, staged in the slave-boy geometry, is the proposed solution. You may reject it; you may not skip the problem. Leading questions versus recollection is the live question.

terms.short: Right belief that can guide action but runs away unless tethered by an account.
terms.definition: The Meno’s statues of Daedalus: true opinion is not yet knowledge. Tethering is understanding why, not a mood of confidence. If virtue were knowledge there should be teachers, yet the great Athenians could not teach their sons. Usefulness in a single action is not stability.

terms.short: From ‘another’s good’ and the tyrant’s happiness to a structural order of city and soul.
terms.definition: Thrasymachus: justice as the advantage of the stronger. Cephalus and Polemarchus fail by counterexample. Plato then constructs justice as each part doing its own work, in the city and analogically in the soul — an analogy that may illustrate rather than prove. Rawls later reopens justice as fairness without the three classes.

terms.short: Reason, spirit, and appetite, each with work, matching the city’s classes.
terms.definition: Justice in a person is the same structural relation as in the city. Gyges had asked why be just if you can be undetected; psychic order is the long answer. The city–soul analogy can smuggle. This is not a modern faculty psychology.

terms.short: Four segments of cognition: images, sensibles, mathematical thought, dialectic of Forms.
terms.definition: The visible and the intelligible are ranked so the Good can be placed: not one more object, but what makes knowable things knowable. The Cave then dramatizes the line as a turning, with a political cost of return.

terms.short: Source of knowability and being — analogically what the sun is to sight.
terms.definition: The Good is not one more Form the way a large fire is one more visible. Education turns the whole soul; the philosopher is compelled back down. Murdoch later recovers a magnetic Good against a naked will — a cousin, not a copy. It is not Thrasymachus’s advantage, and not a utility sum.

terms.short: Education as turning from shadows, and the political cost of going back down.
terms.definition: Prisoners take shadows for the world; release hurts; the sun blinds; return is dangerous. The image is knowledge, politics, and conversion at once. Pair it with the divided line rather than treating it as a detached allegory.

terms.short: This horse, this human: the particular as primary subject — later Descartes’ two substances, Spinoza’s one.
terms.definition: In the Categories, primary substance is neither said of a subject nor in a subject; ‘human’ is secondary. Metaphysics studies being with substance as the focus. Descartes then treats mind and body as really distinct; Spinoza allows only God-or-Nature. Same lemma, three ontologies.

terms.short: Four answers to ‘why?’: material, formal, efficient, final — not four lab events.
terms.definition: A house is bricks, the plan, the builder, and shelter. Nature is an inner principle of motion, unlike art. Final cause cites that-for-the-sake-of-which, not only pushes from behind; hear it first in living things. Form-in-matter is how Aristotle keeps change without Parmenides’ contradiction.

terms.short: Activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, over a complete life — not a mood called happiness.
terms.definition: Pleasure, honor, and wealth are refused as the highest good. ‘Flourishing’ is closer than ‘feeling happy,’ but the Greek still means a complete activity, not a score. The function argument ties this to reason done well. One swallow does not make a spring. Epicurus will offer a rival complete life without civic grandeur.

terms.short: Characteristic work: the human good is rational activity done well.
terms.definition: If a human has a function, it concerns reason, and living well is performing that work excellently. You may reject the idea that we have a function; hear the argument first. It links eudaimonia to virtue as excellence at that work.

terms.short: Excellence: for Aristotle, a stable disposition formed by habituation, aiming at a mean relative to us.
terms.definition: Moral virtue is not a feeling and not a mere capacity. Courage is not half-cowardice; mediocrity is the cartoon of the mean. Plato’s Meno asked whether virtue is knowledge; Aristotle answers with character. Anscombe later reaches back toward this psychology before modern ‘ought’-talk.

terms.short: A stable disposition of character — what habituation produces, and what knowing the mean still lacks.
terms.definition: You can know where the mean lies and still not be virtuous. Hexis is second nature, formed by repeated action. Feelings happen; virtue is how you are disposed toward them.

terms.short: Hitting the mark relative to us, as the prudent person would judge — not a geometric midpoint.
terms.definition: Fear and anger have excess and defect; virtue is the right amount, toward the right people, at the right time. It is not ‘being moderate about everything,’ and not the same quantity for every body. Phronēsis is the eye that finds it.

terms.short: Practical wisdom: the reasoned capacity to hit the mean in action, not a separate rulebook.
terms.definition: The mean is ‘as the phronimos would define it’ because ethics is not geometry. Prudence here is excellence in deliberation about a human life, not cleverness at means to any end. Epicurus praises prudence for a different reason: choosing among pleasures.

terms.short: Knowing the good and not doing it — the ancestor of Augustine’s divided will.
terms.definition: Aristotle treats incontinence as real, against a hard Socratic ‘virtue is knowledge.’ Augustine narrates a will that both wants and does not want conversion, without two natures. Epictetus would say the impression was assented to.

aliases: being is said in many ways
terms.short: ‘Being’ is said in many ways, but around a focus — as ‘healthy’ is said of urine, diet, and the body.
terms.definition: Not a heap of puns, and not a single univocal sense. Substance is the focus; other categories are because of it. That lets Aristotle study being without treating ‘being’ as one more genus like animal.

terms.short: A syllogism from true, primary, immediate premises that give the why — not any persuasive speech.
terms.definition: Scientific knowledge has a shape. If every premise needed demonstration, nothing would be known as science; first principles are known another way. Knowing that differs from knowing why. Averroes and Aquinas reuse the tool inside a revealed or legal frame. Hume will ask what happens if the premises include the future resembling the past.

terms.short: Unperturbedness: Epicurean freedom from empty fear, and the Pyrrhonist’s quiet after suspension.
terms.definition: For Epicurus it comes from classifying desires and seeing that death is nothing to us — prudence, not the banquet. Sextus makes it the point of epochē, not a side effect. Same word, two therapies: one by a true physics, one by refusing dogma.

terms.short: Wants with no natural limit, produced by false beliefs about what we need.
terms.definition: Hunger is natural and necessary; crowns and luxury without limit are empty and cannot be satisfied, so they cannot be the end. This is hedonism as a discipline against frenzy. Ataraxia is the stable result, not a new unlimited want called peace.

terms.short: When we exist, death is not present; when death is present, we do not.
terms.definition: No subject remains to be harmed. Lucretius argues that the soul-compound dissolves, and offers the time before birth as analogue of the time after. A dualist must deny that the soul is bodily in that sense. Whether this shows death is not bad, or only that post-mortem experience is impossible, is the leftover question.

terms.short: Judgment, impulse, desire — as opposed to body, property, reputation, and office.
terms.definition: Freedom sits inside assent. Confusing the two classes is the source of disturbance. It is not a promise that the body will not be harmed, and not a claim that you can make other people’s opinions yours to guarantee. Roles can still bind as duties without making outcomes yours.

terms.short: The free inner yes or no to an impression — where Stoic freedom actually sits.
terms.definition: A troubling appearance need not carry the judgment that the world is bad. Pause and test: is this up to me, and what has my judgment added? Pyrrhonists withhold assent for a different reason: equipollence, not a doctrine of the good. Descartes later makes judgment the site of error when will outruns intellect.

terms.short: Freedom from passions that rest on false valuations — not numbness, and not Epicurean ataraxia.
terms.definition: The ruling faculty does not treat externals as genuine goods or evils. Pathē are misguided impulses; good affective states can remain. The handbooks relocate desire rather than promising a painless body. English ‘apathy’ is a false friend.

terms.short: Suspension of judgment on what is non-evident — the Pyrrhonist’s act, not a secret dogma that nothing is known.
terms.definition: Oppose appearances until they balance; then withhold assent; then quiet. ‘Nothing is known’ would itself be a thesis. The skeptic lives by how things appear — honey tastes sweet — without a criterion of the hidden. Hume’s custom is not this: he walks out of the study and infers.

terms.short: Skepticism as a practice of opposing appearances, aiming at quiet — not Academic ‘nothing can be known.’
terms.definition: It is an ability, not a metaphysics of unreality. It differs from Descartes’ doubt (an instrument for certainty) and from Hume’s custom (we must live by causal inference). Flatten all three into ‘skepticism’ and the sequence goes mute.

terms.short: Beyond being and intellect: the source from which Intellect and Soul proceed without emptying it.
terms.definition: Plotinus’s first hypostasis is not a being among beings and not a committee of gods. Intellect is Forms as thinking and being together; Soul looks both toward Intellect and toward the sensible. The Cave’s ascent becomes procession and conversion of attention.

terms.short: A standing level of reality in Plotinus: One, Intellect, Soul — not a fourth deity.
terms.definition: Hypostases are a metaphysics of procession, not a pantheon. The question is how a unity can be the life of a many. Christian uses of the word for the Trinity are a later story.

terms.short: The mind’s seeing as lit from above — Platonist help toward an incorporeal God, short of a healed will.
terms.definition: Augustine credits Platonist books with an incorporeal God and evil as privation; they do not deliver the Incarnation or conversion. Plotinus’s turn toward Intellect is the pagan cousin. Book VIII then shows what more information cannot do.

terms.short: The wheel of external goods — as opposed to a good that cannot be taken.
terms.definition: Boethius’s Philosophy diagnoses exile as a confusion about what is truly his. Wealth, office, and fame fail of self-sufficiency; beatitude is located in the highest good. The consolation is that argument, not a proverb that everything happens for the best.

terms.short: That for the sake of which other goods are sought — complete; in Boethius, identified with God.
terms.definition: Aristotle already sought a complete, self-sufficient end. Boethius inventories false goods and turns to God. Kant refuses happiness as the unqualified good and names a good will. Mill names utility. Keep the slot, and track what fills it.

terms.short: Evil as a lack of good in something that, as being, still comes from God — not a rival substance.
terms.definition: If God is the source of all that is, evil cannot be a co-eternal stuff. Calling cruelty a privation blocks a two-god cosmology; it does not yet explain why evil weighs on a life. That leftover is why the will must be narrated. ‘Nothing’ is not a joke that suffering is unreal.

terms.short: The power to consent or refuse — Augustine’s drama; later Kant’s practical reason, Schopenhauer’s blind striving.
terms.definition: Augustine: a will that cannot will itself whole, habit as a chain, grace in the story. Descartes locates error in the will’s overreach. Kant’s good will is good without qualification. Schopenhauer names Will as thing-in-itself, not a moral chooser. Murdoch attacks the naked will as the whole of morals. One English word; do not import Kant into Hippo.

terms.short: One agent both wanting and not wanting the same conversion — not a second nature as the Manichees claimed.
terms.definition: Inner conflict without dualist metaphysics. Knowing the good is not doing it; habit binds. The garden scene claims that more information cannot close the will. Two wills here are not two gods.

terms.short: Time as a stretch of the soul: memory, attention, expectation holding past, present, and future.
terms.definition: We speak of past and future, yet the past is no longer and the future is not yet — so where is time? Augustine’s suggestion is a threefold present in the soul, measured as the soul’s own distension. God is not in time the way we are, only longer.

terms.short: Faith seeking understanding — Anselm’s frame, not a replacement of faith by proof.
terms.definition: The Proslogion argues from within belief: ‘that than which nothing greater can be thought’ is prayed, then thought. The argument is clarification and spiritual exercise as much as proof. Aquinas will later set this a priori style aside and start from the world.

terms.short: From the concept of that than which nothing greater can be thought, to extra-mental existence.
terms.definition: Existence in reality is greater than existence in the understanding alone, so the greatest conceivable cannot be only in the intellect. Gaunilo’s lost island asks whether the form proves too much. Descartes retries from essence. Aquinas does not use this as his Five Ways.

terms.short: A discipline of what we may not say of God — names as negations or relations, to protect simplicity.
terms.definition: Maimonides blocks univocal positive attributes that would make God composite or like creatures. If ‘knows’ meant the same in God and in us, we would have imported creaturely structure. Whether this is still knowledge of God, or a rule for silence, is the live question.

terms.short: God-talk that is neither univocal with creatures nor a sheer pun.
terms.definition: After the pressure on attributes, names of God can be ordered to one focus without identical meaning. Aristotle’s focal meaning of being is a cousin, not the same theory. Aquinas’s ‘this we call God’ at the end of a Way assumes some such speech is still possible.

terms.short: God is not composed of parts, matter, or really distinct attributes the way creatures are.
terms.definition: Positive univocal attributes threaten this. Maimonides’ discipline and Aquinas’s ways both orbit simplicity. Spinoza later radicalizes related pressures into one substance with infinite attributes — a different conclusion from the same allergy to composition.

terms.short: Theology as a science that receives its principles from revelation, as subaltern sciences receive theirs from a higher one.
terms.definition: Philosophy can demonstrate some preambles and serve; it does not replace the higher light. If the principles are revealed, in what sense is this still scientia? That is q.1’s question, before q.2’s ways.

terms.short: Five paths from features of the world to a first that all call God — not five ontological arguments.
terms.definition: Motion, causation, contingency, degrees, governance: each way has a middle term and a terminus of explanation. ‘And this we call God’ names; it does not yet deliver the Trinity. A student who says science refuted the first way without stating the first way has skipped the argument.

terms.short: The rational creature’s share in eternal law: good is to be done and pursued, evil avoided.
terms.definition: Law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, by one who has care of the community, promulgated. The first precept of practical reason is specified through natural inclinations — life, knowledge, social life. Passion and custom can obscure particular conclusions. Human law fails as law when it misses reason or the common good.

terms.short: God’s governance of creation — the highest in Aquinas’s hierarchy of eternal, natural, human, and divine law.
terms.definition: Natural law is our share in that governance; human law is particular determination; divine law is revealed. This is not Hobbes’s command of a mortal god, and not Rousseau’s general will, though both later occupy the ‘what makes law law’ slot.

terms.short: Tribe, cave, marketplace, theatre: systematic prejudices that block a new induction.
terms.definition: Bacon diagnoses before he methodizes. The tribe is human nature’s distortions; the cave, the individual’s den; the marketplace, words that muddle even sincere speakers; the theatre, received systems. Quoting a famous name instead of looking is Theatre and Marketplace compounded.

terms.short: Descartes’ rules — evidence, division, order, complete enumerations — plus a provisional morale while the house is down.
terms.definition: Method is a discipline of belief, not a biography of a stove. Provisional morality is a scaffold for living during renovation, not the later metaphysics. Bacon wanted a new organon against idols; Descartes wants certainty. Peirce will later call Cartesian ‘clarity’ a failed way of fixing belief.

terms.short: Withdrawing assent from all that can be doubted — an instrument for certainty, not a lifestyle.
terms.definition: Dreaming undermines sensory belief; a deceiver threatens even mathematics. What survives is the thinking I. This is not Pyrrhonian quiet without a rebuild, and not Hume’s custom. By the end of Meditation II, other bodies are not yet proved.

terms.short: I am, I exist: even if I am deceived, I who am deceived must be.
terms.definition: As Descartes presents it, this is not an inference from ‘everything that thinks exists.’ At this stage I am a thinking thing; the wax shows intellect’s grasp of body still inside a thin ontology. Hegel will refuse a lonely cogito by making self-consciousness social from the start.

terms.short: The mark of truth — once God is no deceiver. The circle: that guarantee seems to use the mark it certifies.
terms.definition: Meditation III’s causal argument for God, IV’s account of error, and the rule of clear and distinct perception stand together. The worry is that such perceptions are reliable only if God exists, while God’s existence is proved by them. A finite mind’s idea of the infinite is the engine of III.

terms.short: The apparent loop: God’s veracity certifies clear and distinct perception, which was used to prove God.
terms.definition: Whether Descartes has a way out is secondary to seeing why the rebuild of knowledge needs a non-deceiving God at all. Meditation IV’s theodicy of error — the will outrunning the intellect — belongs to the same architecture.

terms.short: Mind and body are really distinct, clearly conceivable apart — yet I am also a union that senses.
terms.definition: God can bring about what is clearly conceived; matter is extension; bodies exist; the leftover problem is the living composite. ‘Only mind’ and ‘only machine’ both miss Meditation VI. Hobbes will start from bodies; Locke from ideas.

terms.short: The essence of matter for Descartes: spatial spread, excluding weight and color as intrinsic.
terms.definition: The wax’s sensory qualities change; what remains is grasped by intellect as extended, flexible, changeable. Physics becomes a geometry of extension, which is why secondary qualities later become a problem for Locke and Berkeley.

terms.short: What is in another and conceived through another — a finite thing, for Spinoza, not a rival substance.
terms.definition: Substance is in itself and conceived through itself; there is only one, God-or-Nature. Finite things are modes. Descartes’ created substances are refused. Leibniz will multiply windowless substances instead.

terms.short: What intellect perceives of substance as constituting its essence — for Spinoza, thought and extension among infinitely many.
terms.definition: Attributes are how we conceive the one substance, not parts glued on. Descartes had two created-substance essences; Spinoza has one substance infinitely attributed. Maimonides had already worried that creaturely attributes fracture God.

terms.short: God or Nature: one substance, no lawgiving will that might have done otherwise.
terms.definition: Everything follows from the divine nature; ‘could have been otherwise’ is a defect of imagination. Final causes are refused. Prayer, miracle, and a king-like free will do not survive. Conatus is how modes live this necessity.

terms.short: Each thing’s striving to persevere in its being — Spinoza’s physics of affect under necessity.
terms.definition: Not a Cartesian free will, and not an Epicurean ataraxia project. Modes exist by endeavoring. Schopenhauer’s Will is a later, darker cousin: thing-in-itself as striving.

terms.short: Under uncertainty, living as if God exists dominates if the gain is infinite — not a fifth Way.
terms.definition: Pascal’s fragment is a practical argument, inside humility about the God of the philosophers versus Abraham. Custom and habituation are how one comes to believe; the Wager does not replace a life. It does not demonstrate God as a triangle is demonstrated.

terms.short: A simple, windowless substance whose inner states unfold from its complete concept.
terms.definition: No genuine influx of accidents from outside. Not all monads are minds like ours. Pre-established harmony is how mind and body agree without pushing. This answers Spinoza’s one substance by multiplying simples, and Descartes’ union without occasionalist miracles at every turn.

terms.short: Created substances’ programs correspond from the start — no influx, no constant divine patching.
terms.definition: Mind and body agree because God chose a world of corresponding unfolding, not because thought is a product of shove. It is a thesis about causation among substances, not a claim that life feels harmonious.

terms.short: The human condition without a common power — Hobbes’s war from equality; Locke’s already lawful condition with property.
terms.definition: Hobbes: equality of vulnerability plus the right of nature makes preemption rational. Locke: a law of nature and labor-property before the magistrate. Rousseau conjectures a different natural independence. None of these is a camping trip. Ask whether you are reading history, thought experiment, or warning.

terms.short: Hobbes: liberty to use power for life — distinct from a law of nature, which is a precept: seek peace.
terms.definition: Right is liberty; law binds. The first laws: seek peace, and be willing to lay down right when others do. Covenants without the sword are words. Locke’s ‘law of nature’ is already moral-theological in a way Hobbes’s rational precepts are not.

terms.short: Each makes the sovereign the bearer of their person — a real unity, not a mere crowd.
terms.definition: The sovereign’s acts are yours. Subjects cannot accuse that person of injustice in the covenant’s terms. Liberty remaining is mainly the silence of the law plus defense of life. Locke’s trust can be withdrawn when power exceeds right — a different metaphysics.

terms.short: Locke’s title to property: mixing labor with the common, within spoilage and ‘enough and as good.’
terms.definition: Money relaxes the original limits by consent to unequal possession. Political society is by consent, not Hobbesian authorization that cannot be withdrawn. This is not ‘whatever I touch is mine.’

terms.short: Principles stamped on the mind from birth — Locke’s target: teaching explains the appearance of them.
terms.definition: Even universal consent would not prove innateness; children lack the supposed maxims. ‘White paper’ does not mean no faculties. A disposition to form an idea is not the idea. Descartes’ innate idea of God is in the dock.

terms.short: Whatever is before the mind when a person thinks — from sensation and reflection, not Plato’s Form.
terms.definition: Simple ideas are not made by us at will. Berkeley will make ideas plus spirits the furniture of unthinking things; Hume will split impression and idea by force and liveliness. When the course says ‘idea,’ check whether you are in Republic VI or in the Essay.

terms.short: Bulk, figure, motion, number, solidity — inseparable from body, resembling our ideas of them, on Locke’s telling.
terms.definition: Secondary qualities are powers to produce sensations that do not resemble those ideas in the object as yellow is in the idea. Descartes had already made extension the essence of matter. Berkeley will deny the material substratum supposed to hold the powers.

terms.short: Powers in bodies to produce sensations — real as powers, not ‘in the object’ as the idea of yellow is yellow.
terms.definition: Color is not nothing, and not a miniature yellow painted on the corpuscle. The resemblance problem is already visible and will feed Berkeley and Hume. Whether the world is colorless unobserved is Locke’s edge; Berkeley answers by dropping matter.

aliases: to be is to be perceived
terms.short: For unthinking things, to be is to be perceived — matter as inert substratum does no work.
terms.definition: An apple is a collection of ideas; a triangle that is neither equilateral nor scalene is a fiction. This is not solipsism: spirits and God sustain the order of ideas. The vanishing-furniture joke ignores divine perception. Berkeley abolishes a philosopher’s extra object, not the world of common life.

terms.short: The lively perception — sensation or feeling — of which simple ideas are copies.
terms.definition: Where an alleged idea has no impression, suspect a confusion. The missing shade of blue is the famous apparent exception; note it, don’t let it erase the rule. ‘Power,’ ‘necessary connexion,’ and a simple self will be run through this test.

terms.short: Simple ideas are copies of impressions — Hume’s meaning-test for philosophical terms.
terms.definition: Complex ideas may be compounded; the discipline is on empty terms. This prepares causation: hunt the impression of necessity. Peirce’s pragmatic maxim is a later, different test: conceivable practical effects.

terms.short: Demonstrative truths (geometry, arithmetic) — as opposed to matters of fact, whose contraries remain conceivable.
terms.definition: Causal claims about the unobserved are matters of fact, and the inference from observed to unobserved is not itself a demonstration. Kant will rename a nearby cut analytic/synthetic and a priori/a posteriori. Quine will attack the analytic/synthetic dogma.

terms.short: Not insight into a glue in objects: constant conjunction plus the mind’s determination.
terms.definition: Hume does not tell you to stop inferring; he tells you what the inference is. Custom is the guide of life. Kant’s Copernican preface names this interruption of dogmatic metaphysics. Pre-established harmony was an earlier answer to a different causal problem.

terms.short: The instinct by which we infer from past to future — Hume’s replacement for a demonstration of induction.
terms.definition: Limit inquiry to what custom and experience support, without Pyrrhonian refusal to live. Science still works after necessity is relocated to the mind’s feeling — not because we have pierced essences. Mill’s ‘despotism of custom’ is a different, political use of the word.

terms.short: The impression we actually have: a feeling of determination after custom, projected onto the world.
terms.definition: We do not see the glue. If necessity is in the mind, science still works because custom is reliable enough for life. Kant will try to save necessity as a condition of possible experience. Hume does not ‘deny causation’ if that means denying this idea of secret power.

terms.short: The inference from ‘this has happened’ to ‘it will’ — not a theorem of experience, and not a demonstration.
terms.definition: Hume poses the problem; Russell names a principle we cannot prove from experience and cannot do without. It is a postulate of knowledge, not a confession that we should stop expecting sunrise. Aristotle’s induction toward first principles is a different tool.

terms.short: A violation of the laws of nature as uniform experience establishes them — Hume’s bar for testimony.
terms.definition: Testimony is insufficient unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact. This is a rule of evidence, not a laboratory disproof of every report, and not ‘any surprise.’ Spinoza had already made miracles unintelligible inside necessary Nature.

terms.short: What makes a person the same over time — Locke: consciousness; Hume: a bundle and a fiction of imagination.
terms.definition: Locke’s person is forensic, for reward and punishment, not a hidden soul-substance as such. Hume finds no constant impression of self; resembling perceptions are mistaken for one object. Du Bois later splits the first person under a veil — another structure, not Hume’s theatre.

terms.short: The mind as particular perceptions — no simple continuing self distinct from them.
terms.definition: Hume reports introspection and explains why we feign identity. It is not a joke that no one is home. Locke’s forensic person is a rival picture, not a substance Hume failed to find.

terms.short: From order in nature, analogically, to a mind like an artisan — underdetermined, says Philo.
terms.definition: Cleanthes infers a designer proportioned to the effect; Philo multiplies analogies and lets evil constrain what we may infer. The Dialogues do not simply prove atheism; they limit natural religion. This is not Anselm, and not Aquinas’s first mover.

terms.short: Comparative self-love that needs others’ eyes — not mere self-preservation (amour de soi).
terms.definition: Natural man, in Rousseau’s conjecture, has limited needs and pity; moral inequality is largely historical. Amour-propre arrives with socialization. Hobbes’s war is refused as original fact. This is not a field report on one tribe.

terms.short: The common interest the compact creates — not a poll of private appetites.
terms.definition: Legitimacy, not force as right. Alienation to the whole is supposed to produce a moral body whose will you obey as your own. Sovereignty is that will’s exercise; government is not the same thing. ‘Forced to be free’ is education into citizenship, or a threat — hear the paradox.

terms.short: The sum of particular wills — factions and private interest, which the general will is not.
terms.definition: A vote can express the will of all and miss the common interest. Mixing the two is the usual misreading. This is not Mill’s harm principle, and not a utilitarian sum, though all three concern many persons.

terms.short: Fellow-feeling produced by imagining ourselves in another’s situation — Smith’s basis of moral sentiment.
terms.definition: Propriety is correspondence of sentiment; the impartial spectator grows from this mirroring. It is not pity only, not Hobbesian glory, and not Kant’s law. Do not import a cartoon ‘economic man’ from the Wealth of Nations into this opening.

terms.short: The internalized gaze by which we judge our own passions — grown from ordinary spectatorship.
terms.definition: Smith’s device for how morality can be more than a clique’s taste. Whether it can ever be more than a culture’s average gaze is the live question. Rawls’s veil is a cousin only in being a point of view; it is not a theory of moral sentiment.

terms.short: Objects conform to our way of knowing — rather than the mind copying things in themselves.
terms.definition: A research program for how a priori knowledge of objects is possible. Space, time, and the categories are on the subject’s side; knowledge is of appearances; room is made for faith regarding what cannot be known theoretically. Hume interrupted dogmatic necessity; Kant relocates it.

terms.short: Independent of this or that experience — not ‘innate’ in Locke’s sense, and not automatically analytic.
terms.definition: Kant’s four boxes: analytic/synthetic crossed with a priori/a posteriori. The famous problem is the synthetic a priori. Hume’s fork is the provocation. Quine’s holism later threatens the analytic/synthetic cut that keeps the boxes tidy. ‘A priori’ is not a compliment meaning ‘obvious.’

terms.short: Predicate contained in the subject versus adding to it — Kant’s cut; Quine’s first dogma.
terms.definition: Kant needs the cut to pose the synthetic a priori. Quine argues that synonymy, definition, and necessity circle rather than ground analyticity, and that reductionism is a second dogma. If the cut goes, Kant’s architecture is among the casualties. Hume’s fork is an ancestor, not the same tool.

terms.short: Appearance as object of possible experience — what we can know, for Kant, as opposed to the thing in itself.
terms.definition: Knowledge is of phenomena. Schopenhauer calls this side the world as representation, then names Will as thing-in-itself. Husserl’s phenomenology (the unit before Heidegger) is a later method, not Kant’s pair. Keep the word tagged to the first Critique unless a later sitting says otherwise.

terms.short: The thing in itself, thinkable as a limit — not knowable as an object given to us.
terms.definition: Denying knowledge of noumena makes room for faith, and for freedom as practical. Schopenhauer claims to name the noumenon Will — whether that violates Kant’s ban is the question. Noumenon is not Russell’s sense-datum, not Plato’s Form, and not Heidegger’s being.

terms.short: The only thing good without qualification — even if it achieves nothing.
terms.definition: Talents and gifts of fortune can be bad without it. Happiness is refused as the unqualified good. Moral worth attaches to action from duty, not merely in accordance with duty. A person who enjoys helping can still act from duty; the analysis isolates the motive. This is not Schopenhauer’s Will.

terms.short: A means–end rule: if you will the end, you ought to will the means.
terms.definition: The moral law is not hypothetical. Prudence — how to be happy — is. Technical imperatives likewise. Confusing these with the categorical imperative is the usual muddle. Mill’s utility looks, to a Kantian, like a vast hypothetical of happiness.

terms.short: Unconditional: act only on a maxim you can will as universal law, and treat humanity always as an end.
terms.definition: Section I arrives at universal law from common moral cognition; Section II unpacks formulas as supposedly equivalent accents. False promising is the mere-means test. It is not advice about what typically produces happiness. Kierkegaard’s Abraham will collide with this universal.

terms.short: Treat humanity in yourself and others always as an end, never merely as a means.
terms.definition: Not a ban on all cooperation: using someone’s skills with their possible consent is not ‘mere’ means. A lying promise uses another’s agency as a tool. Whether this is a different insight from universal law, or the same law in another accent, is the question.

terms.short: The will’s property of being a law to itself — as opposed to heteronomy.
terms.definition: Not ‘doing whatever you feel.’ Legislators gathered in a kingdom of ends. Political autonomy talk later is a descendant, not this definition. Heteronomy includes both appetite and a merely external command as the source of the principle.

terms.short: The will’s principle taken from something other than its own law — inclination, expected happiness, or alien authority.
terms.definition: A hypothetical imperative is heteronomous when it borrows its law from an object. Divine command, if the law is merely another’s will, is heteronomy — which is why the Euthyphro problem still matters, and why Anscombe will say a modern ‘ought’ looks like a law without a lawgiver.

terms.short: Self-consciousness that needs another: each wants to be acknowledged as not a mere thing.
terms.definition: The struggle, the unequal roles, the lord’s unstable dependence on a reduced other, the bondsman’s work as the engine of a new self. Independent self-consciousness is not achieved by ignoring others — a break with a lonely cogito. Later political uses of ‘recognition’ are related, not identical.

terms.short: ‘The world is my idea’: object for a subject — Kant’s phenomena radicalized.
terms.definition: Then Will as the inner, thing-in-itself, blind striving; intellect is its instrument. This is not Locke’s idea, not the Tractatus’s logical picture, and not Berkeley’s theistic immaterialism. Suffering follows if will is endless.

terms.short: The standard of right: happiness as pleasure and absence of pain of all concerned, with higher and lower kinds.
terms.definition: Not a cartoon of swine. Quality is identified by competent judges who know both kinds. The standard is the general happiness, not a private clique. Kant sees a hypothetical of happiness; Mill sees a rival first word for ethics.

terms.short: Pleasures of a kind competent judges prefer — Mill’s test of quality, not intensity alone.
terms.definition: The ranking is comparative verdict, not a priestly list. Whether competent judges smuggle a non-utilitarian ranking of lives is the live question. This is how Mill answers ‘a doctrine worthy of swine.’

terms.short: Power may be exercised over a member of a civilized community, against their will, only to prevent harm to others.
terms.definition: Not offense, not paternalism for adults as such. Silencing an opinion robs the human race whether the opinion is true or false. ‘Harm’ may expand on demand. Self-regarding faults are not crimes. Individuality then says why liberty is a social good, not only non-interference with trade.

terms.short: Experiments in living as an ingredient of well-being and progress — against the despotism of custom.
terms.definition: Eccentricity is not automatically virtue; frozen types block the competition of ways of life. A utilitarian who crushes the eccentric for majority happiness has failed Mill’s own chapter. The harm principle still binds: individuality is not a right to injure.

terms.short: Abraham’s relation to Isaac cannot be justified in universal ethical language — a private absolute duty to God.
terms.definition: The knight of faith versus the tragic hero who remains in the ethical. Silence matters because language is the ethical’s medium. This refuses Hegelian mediation and collides with Kantian universal law. Distinguishable from a murderer only by an inner we cannot see — that is the terror.

terms.short: The Manifesto’s structure of history: oppressor and oppressed, simplified into bourgeoisie and proletariat.
terms.definition: The bourgeoisie constantly revolutionizes production and produces its own grave-diggers. Communism targets bourgeois property as class property, not every personal appropriation. Political power is organized power of one class. Hegel’s bondsman-labor becomes world-historical.

terms.short: The ruling ideas of an age as the ideas of the ruling class — consciousness shaped by material relations.
terms.definition: Legal and religious ideas that present particular interests as universal. The German Ideology is not assigned; stay with the pamphlet’s frame. Species-being is the neighboring anthropology of productive life.

terms.short: Humanity as productive, social life — the anthropology behind abolishing bourgeois property.
terms.definition: The phrase is from writings this course does not host; the Manifesto sitting is class struggle and a program. Use it for what wage-labor is said to alienate. A materialist will tell Sartre this is what existentialist freedom misses: conditions, class, metabolism with nature.

terms.short: A history of morals that explains values by their descent — not a proof that they are false.
terms.definition: Good/bad versus good/evil; ressentiment as creative; bad conscience as internalized cruelty. If the genealogy is true, does it refute the values or only explain them? Foucault later applies a genealogical sitting to prisons. This is not Aristotle’s genus-and-species.

aliases: good and evil vs good and bad
terms.short: Creative revenge in valuation: the weak invert noble good/bad into good/evil that brands the strong as evil.
terms.definition: Two pairs of terms; mixing them is the usual error. Ressentiment is not a mere complaint; it produces a new table of values. Not a medical diagnosis, and not resentment as a passing mood.

terms.short: Instincts that cannot discharge outwardly turn inward — interiority as a historical product.
terms.definition: The promise-making animal needed a memory made of pain; then internalization. Guilt as a creditor–debtor story, not a timeless fact of reason. The sovereign individual who may promise is an achievement, not a given.

terms.short: Life as interpretive force and command — not a cartoon of domination, and not Kant’s good will.
terms.definition: The assigned Genealogy and Gay Science teach revaluation and the death of God more than a compiled notebook titled Will to Power. Hear it as the psychology of valuation those essays imply: values are instituted, not found as Plato’s Good.

terms.short: The Christian-Platonic horizon of meaning has collapsed — an event in us whose consequences are not yet absorbed.
terms.definition: The madman announces unreadiness, not a weather report and not only a jab at priests. What values and sciences still presuppose the dead God? Hume on miracles is a different argument. The Tractatus’s silence and Murdoch’s Good are later, rival responses to a thinned sky.

terms.short: The meaning of a conception lies in the practical effects we conceive the object to have.
terms.definition: Belief is a habit of action; doubt irritates; inquiry settles. Hardness is a conception of would-be interactions, not a Cartesian inner glow. This does not yet say ‘true means useful this afternoon.’ Descartes’ clear-and-distinct fails the test if it has no conceivable bearings.

terms.short: An idea’s truth as what can be assimilated, corroborated, lived — not the later positivist slogan as a hosted text.
terms.definition: James: truth happens to an idea; it is verified in leading and working, fenced by other truths and the long run. Peirce’s maxim is the ancestor. The Tractatus pictures possible states of affairs — a different tool. Do not parody James as ‘whatever pleases me is true.’

terms.short: When an option is living, forced, and momentous, and intellect cannot decide, it can be lawful to believe ahead of proof.
terms.definition: James against Clifford’s ‘always wait.’ Friendship and religion are the examples, not next week’s weather. Waiting is already a bet. It sits in tension with Peirce’s method of science. Pascal’s Wager is a cousin under uncertainty.

terms.short: Shift philosophy from a museum of ultimate being toward experimental, social intelligence.
terms.definition: Inherited problems are historically rooted in clashes of custom and new knowledge, then asked whether they still serve. Spectator theories of knowing versus doing are the dualism to undo. This is relocation of philosophy’s office, not a denial of science.

terms.short: The sense of always looking at oneself through the eyes of a white world — two-ness, not low self-esteem.
terms.definition: A structure of self-knowledge under domination. The Veil splits worlds of meaning and recognition. It complicates Locke’s and Hume’s first-person self. Whether it is only a wound, or also a way of knowing what the veil hides from others, is the question.

terms.short: The barrier that splits worlds of seeing and being seen — lived segregation of experience.
terms.definition: Du Bois uses the image as analysis. The color-line is a world-historical structure, not a failure of manners. Distinct from Rawls’s veil of ignorance, a device for choosing principles. Same English word, different tools.

terms.short: Identifying good with some natural property — for Moore, a failed analysis of a simple non-natural property.
terms.definition: Good is simple and indefinable; ‘good = pleasure’ remains an open question. It does not mean never mention nature in ethics. Mill’s ‘pleasure is good’ would be tautological if it were an analysis, which Moore denies it successfully is.

terms.short: For any proposed ‘good = X,’ it remains an intelligible question whether X is good — so the analysis fails.
terms.definition: Moore’s test of definitions. You may reject it as a linguistic habit; you must state it. Pair it with the naturalistic fallacy; they are the same campaign. Not a proof that ethics is impossible.

terms.short: The color-patch, hardness, and so on immediately present — what Russell says we are acquainted with, not yet the public table.
terms.definition: Appearance versus the physicist’s object. Idealism is a live option he will not simply swallow. Knowledge by description then bridges to other minds and to physics. This is not Berkeley’s whole ontology, and not Kant’s structured phenomenon.

terms.short: Direct presentation — sense-data, perhaps oneself — as opposed to knowledge by description of what we are not given.
terms.definition: Russell’s way out of the table problem. Logically proper names would attach to what we are acquainted with; ordinary names work by descriptions. On Denoting is not assigned; use the Problems chapters’ frame.

terms.short: Knowing an object as ‘the so-and-so’ when we are not acquainted with it.
terms.definition: Without this, sense-data trap you in a private show. Definite descriptions do the work of reaching the table and other minds. It is a hypothesis about how science gets beyond appearance, not a refutation of Berkeley by force.

terms.short: A phrase of the form ‘the F’ — how we talk about what we are not acquainted with.
terms.definition: It picks uniquely, or fails, rather than naming by baptism. Ordinary names, for this Russell, are truncated descriptions. Kripke’s later causal-historical names are a map-item, not this sitting.

terms.short: A name whose meaning is the object of acquaintance — not an ordinary proper name that works by descriptions.
terms.definition: Ordinary names are truncated descriptions; a logically proper name would require direct presentation. That is how Russell tries to keep contact with reality without claiming we are acquainted with physical objects. Later Wittgenstein loosens naming as the whole story of meaning.

terms.short: A proposition shares logical form with a possible state of affairs — it shows how things stand if true.
terms.definition: The world is the totality of facts, not of things. Sense is a possible situation, not a psychological association. Logical form cannot be said in the same way; it shows. Ethics and the mystical are not additional facts among facts.

terms.short: What can be shown cannot be said — logical form, ethics, the mystical; the book itself is a ladder to throw away.
terms.definition: Elucidations to be discarded once one has seen the world rightly. Proposition 7 is a rule, not a poetic sigh. If the book is nonsense by its own light, why read it? A second Wittgenstein will change pictures and the dream of a final silence.

terms.short: A comparison: looking at primitive practices of using words, to loosen the grip of one picture.
terms.definition: The shopkeeper and the five red apples crack ‘words as names of objects.’ Meaning as use is mastery of a technique in a practice, not ‘words mean whatever I like.’ This repudiates the Tractatus picture theory without being a theory of everything.

terms.short: Understanding a word is often knowing how to go on in a practice — not always having a mental picture of an object.
terms.definition: The Augustinian picture (word to object) is the target. Use is public technique, with criteria; it is not a private pointing that needs no public check. Family resemblance then warns against one hidden essence behind all uses of ‘game.’

terms.short: A warning against assuming one essence hidden behind all uses of a word — not a biological taxonomy of concepts.
terms.definition: Overlapping similarities (games) replace a single Form of Game. Safer as a warning against theories of concepts than as a new theory of concepts. It is not a return to Plato’s eidos.

terms.short: Consciousness as consciousness-of — directedness is primitive, not a sealed inner theatre that later gets related to objects.
terms.definition: An object can be intended even when it does not exist as a real thing. Aboutness is not a copy in the mind. Descartes’ cogito can look like a thinking substance first; this sitting makes of-ness first.

aliases: general thesis of the natural attitude
terms.short: The default general thesis that the world is simply there — not a theory you adopted.
terms.definition: Living in it is not a philosophical choice. The epoché suspends that thesis without a skeptical denial that the world exists. Distinct from Kant’s phenomenon and from Russell’s sense-data as a starting inventory.

terms.short: Suspending the natural attitude’s general thesis — without Pyrrhonian quiet, and without Cartesian doubt as a hunt for a thinking substance.
terms.definition: The world is not denied; the thesis that it simply is is put out of play so the intended as such can be described. Not Sextus’s epochē, not Meditation I’s deceiver. Gibson 1931 is still in US copyright until 2027.

terms.short: The act-side of intentional consciousness — intending as an act, correlative with a noema.
terms.definition: Not a little performance inside a box. If you split noesis and noema into two substances, you have missed the correlation. Distinct from Anaxagoras’s Nous as a cosmic arranger.

terms.short: The object-as-meant — the intended as such, not a little object in the head and not automatically a real thing in nature.
terms.definition: A psychologistic reading makes the noema a mental picture; Husserl refuses that. The tree as perceived is not a second tree in consciousness.

terms.short: The a priori grasp of essences — what phenomenology claims to be a science of, against psychologism’s empirical mental events.
terms.definition: Not a return to Plato’s separate Forms, and not Aristotle’s form-in-matter as a cause of change. The word names a method of seeing what must belong to an intentional act as such.

terms.short: The entity we are, whose being is an issue for it — the one that understands being, not a Cartesian subject with properties first.
terms.definition: The forgotten question is being; Dasein is the being that can ask it. Existence here is ours, not a list of attributes of a thing. Russell’s table would look different if the first question were being, not sense-data. The assigned move is the Introduction, not the whole book.

terms.short: Being is not a being among beings — pointing to God, nature, or the subject does not answer what it means to be.
terms.definition: Forgetfulness of that difference is the diagnosis. Method and subject-matter: ontology via the being that asks. This is not a mineral in an inventory, not Parmenides’ sphere as cosmology only, and not Kant’s noumenon.

terms.short: There is no maker’s blueprint that tells you in advance what you ought to be.
terms.definition: In choosing, you choose an image of the human, hence anguish; offered as a humanism against quietism. ‘Choosing for all’ may smuggle a Kantian universal without the moral law. A materialist asks what conditions this freedom misses.

terms.short: Fleeing the burden of having to invent oneself — self-excuse, not a synonym for lying.
terms.definition: The lecture stresses anguish and answers the charge that existentialism excuses doing nothing. Bad faith names citing a ready-made nature, or treating oneself as a thing. Distinct from Nietzschean bad conscience, which is internalized cruelty.

terms.short: The analytic/synthetic distinction, and reduction of each statement to a sensory confirming range.
terms.definition: Synonymy does not easily save analyticity: definition and necessity circle. Statements meet experience as a corporate body; any statement can be held true if we adjust elsewhere. Holism is a picture of science, not automatically Pyrrhonism. Kant’s synthetic a priori is among the stakes.

terms.short: Experience judges a corporate body of statements — revision can strike anywhere if we make enough adjustments.
terms.definition: Not ‘anything goes,’ and not a claim that science never revises. Contrast Aristotle’s demonstration from first principles, Hume’s sentence-level custom, and Popper’s sharp clash with basic statements. The question is whether this is skepticism or a picture of science.

terms.short: Evidence does not pick out a unique theory — more than one adjustment of the web can save the appearances.
terms.definition: As Quine uses it: any statement can be held true if we make enough changes elsewhere. Not a proof that science is arbitrary, and not Popper’s isolated falsifying basic statement. Duhem is in the ancestry.

terms.short: A theory is scientific only if it risks clash with some possible basic statement — it forbids something, rather than waiting on confirming instances.
terms.definition: Demarcation by falsifiability, not verification. Ad hoc immunization is a danger. Not Hume’s induction made certain, and not a hagiography of lab practice. Kuhn’s normal science will look unlike a daily hunt for refutations.

terms.short: How to mark science off from metaphysics and from merely confirming story-telling — not how to justify induction as Hume demanded.
terms.definition: Induction is restated, then refused as a demand for the unjustifiable. Falsifiability is the proposed criterion. Verification by accumulating positives is what is being replaced.

terms.short: The exemplary achievement that trains what counts as a puzzle — not a synonym for ‘theory,’ and not a mere list of propositions.
terms.definition: Normal science is puzzle-solving under it. Revolutions change world-views rather than cumulatively approaching one neutral language. Incommensurability is the sting. Read after Popper and Quine in this course.

terms.short: Puzzle-solving under a paradigm — not perpetual revolution, and not a daily hunt for falsifying instances as the whole business.
terms.definition: The community is trained into what counts as a solution. Contrast a naive Popperian calendar of conjecture-and-refutation. Anomaly is fuller in later chapters if you read on.

terms.short: Rival paradigms may not share a fully neutral observation language — communication across a revolution is not a simple translation.
terms.definition: Not a claim that no argument is possible, and not a proof that science is fashion. It sits uneasily with Popper’s clash and with Quine’s one web facing one tribunal.

terms.short: A law-sense leftover from a divine-law ethics, now without a lawgiver — incoherent as modern moral philosophy uses it.
terms.definition: Anscombe wants ethics laid aside until we have an adequate philosophy of psychology. She targets both thin duty-talk and a certain consequentialism. Aristotle’s hexis is in the offing, not a slogan ‘be like Aristotle.’ This does not refute every sentence of the Groundwork; it diagnoses a classroom ‘ought.’

terms.short: A point of view, not a place: parties behind a veil of ignorance choose principles for the basic structure.
terms.definition: Justice as fairness: a Kantian procedure with economic content, rival to utilitarianism. The veil screens morally irrelevant bargaining advantages. Two principles in order: equal basic liberties, then inequalities to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. Not Hobbes’s war, not a 1776 assembly.

terms.short: The screen in the original position: no knowledge of one’s class, talents, or conception of the good as a bargaining chip.
terms.definition: A device for fairness, not Du Bois’s Veil of lived split worlds. Whether it is a moral insight or an economic thought experiment is the question. Mill’s harm principle may already include some liberties the first principle lists.

aliases: greatest benefit of the least advantaged
terms.short: Social and economic inequalities are just only if they most benefit the least advantaged.
terms.definition: Not simple equality, not maximax for the gifted. Inequalities can be just if they raise the worst off compared with a more equal scheme. Utilitarian sacrifice of the few as a mere sum is what the parties would not choose.

terms.short: Perpetual possible visibility as a diagram of modern power — producing self-discipline, not only forbidding acts.
terms.definition: Bentham’s plan becomes a figure of schools, barracks, prisons. Power is productive and capillary, unlike Hobbes’s spectacular sword. A fair worry: a prison plan overextended into a theory of modernity.

terms.short: Power that makes subjects, visibilities, and what counts as knowable — not only a sovereign’s right to say no.
terms.definition: The assigned chapter’s productive power and internalized gaze are the handle. Distinct from Hobbesian authorization and from Rawls’s principles chosen by unsituated parties. Study the diagram, not a biography.

terms.short: Moral activity as a just and loving gaze that can change what is there to be seen — without a new public act.
terms.definition: Against existentialist or Kantian will as the whole of morals. Unselfing is the work. The Good is magnetic, not chosen like a brand. A cousin of the Cave, not a copy; a cousin of Smith’s spectator, not a sentiment theory.

terms.short: A transcendent, magnetic orientation of the soul — Platonic without cheap mysticism, against a naked will.
terms.definition: Murdoch’s reply to Sartre and to a certain analytic thinness. Not Mill’s competent judges, not the difference principle, not Nietzsche’s death of God as the last word. Moore’s simple ‘good’ is a different, thinner object. Whether this is the Cave you already had, or a new use of it, is the question.

terms.short: Justified true belief is not sufficient for knowledge — cases where luck breaks the analysis.
terms.definition: The map pin: justification versus knowledge, after Plato’s Meno already distinguished true opinion from knowledge. It is not a proof that no one knows anything. Name a legal next text; do not paste the article into the app.
